cases.query: ⟨x,x⟩=‖x‖ for all x
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ with x=2, the inner product is 4 and the norm is 2.

cases.query: |⟨x,y⟩|=‖x‖‖y‖ for all x,y
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ², x=e₁ and y=e₂ give 0 on the left and 1 on the right.

cases.query: ‖x+y‖²=‖x‖²+‖y‖² without orthogonality
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ, x=y=1 gives 4 versus 2.

cases.query: The parallelogram identity holds in every normed space
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² with the ℓ¹ norm, x=e₁,y=e₂ give left side 8 and right side 4. An inner-product norm is necessary.

cases.query: 2⟨x,y⟩=‖x+y‖²-‖x-y‖²
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ, x=y=1 gives 2 versus 4.

cases.query: Every pairwise orthogonal family is independent, even with zero vectors
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The one-element family consisting of zero is pairwise orthogonal but linearly dependent.

cases.query: Bessel inequality holds for every linearly independent family
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ, the one-vector family v₀=2 is independent; x=1 gives coefficient square 4>1.

cases.query: S≤T implies S⊥≤T⊥
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ, S={0}, T=ℝ give S⊥=ℝ and T⊥={0}.

cases.query: Double orthogonal complement equals S for every nonclosed infinite-dimensional subspace
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The finite-support sequences in ℓ² are dense and proper; their orthogonal complement is zero, so the double complement is all ℓ².
In ℝ² take S=span e₁ and T=span e₂. The left side is zero and the right side is all ℝ².

cases.query: dim S=dim S⊥ for every S
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ³ take S=span e₁. The two dimensions are 1 and 2.

cases.query: S+T=V implies S∩T={0}
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Taking S=T=ℝ gives sum ℝ but intersection ℝ.

cases.query: x-P_S x always belongs to S
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ², let S=span e₁ and x=e₂. The residual is e₂, outside S.

cases.query: y∈S alone implies P_S x=y
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ, S=ℝ, x=0,y=1. Membership holds but the projection is 0. The orthogonal-residual premise is necessary.

cases.query: P_S x=x iff x∈S⊥
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ with S=ℝ and x=1, x is fixed but does not belong to S⊥={0}.

cases.query: Every linear map is idempotent
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℝ let f(x)=2x. Then f(f(1))=4≠2=f(1).

cases.query: P_S x=0 iff x∈S
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² with S=span e₁ and x=e₂, the projection is zero but x∉S.

cases.query: ‖P_S x‖<‖x‖ for every nonzero x
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Choose any nonzero x∈S; then P_S x=x and equality holds.

cases.query: P_(S⊥) x=P_S x for every S,x
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² take S=span e₁ and x=e₁. The two projections are 0 and e₁.

cases.query: P_S(P_T x)=P_S x without S≤T
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² take S=span e₁, T=span e₂, x=e₁. The left side is zero and the right side is e₁.

cases.query: Every idempotent real operator is symmetric
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The matrix [[1,1],[0,0]] is idempotent. For x=e₂,y=e₁, ⟨Px,y⟩=1 whereas ⟨x,Py⟩=0.
In ℝ² take S=span e₁ and x=e₁+e₂. The left side is √2 and the right side is 2.

cases.query: ‖P_S x‖=‖x‖ for every x
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² take S=span e₁ and x=e₂. The projected norm is 0 and the original norm is 1.

cases.query: ‖x-P_S x‖≤‖x-y‖ for arbitrary y∈V
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ with S={0}, take x=y=1. The left side is 1 and the right side is 0; y∈S is essential.

cases.query: GramSchmidt(v) is orthonormal without normalization
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For the one-vector family v₀=2 in ℝ, Gram–Schmidt returns 2, which is not a unit vector.

cases.query: GramSchmidt(v) spans the ambient space for every v
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² the one-vector family e₁ and its Gram–Schmidt output both span only a line.

cases.query: GramSchmidt(v) is independent for every input family
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For v₀=v₁=e₁, the second Gram–Schmidt vector is zero.

cases.query: Normalized GramSchmidt(v) is orthonormal even for dependent v
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For v₀=v₁=e₁, the second normalized output remains zero and has norm 0, not 1.

cases.query: Normalized GramSchmidt(v)=v for all independent v
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For the one-vector family v₀=2 in ℝ, the normalized output is 1, although both families have the same span.

cases.query: GramSchmidt(v)=v whenever v is independent
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ², v₀=e₁,v₁=e₁+e₂ are independent. The second output is e₂, not e₁+e₂.

cases.query: The orthonormal expansion reconstructs x using an arbitrary orthonormal family
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² the one-vector family e₁ is orthonormal, but x=e₂ has all its coefficients zero and is not reconstructed.

cases.query: Parseval equality holds for every orthonormal family, not necessarily spanning
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ² take the one-vector family e₁ and x=e₂. The coefficient-square sum is 0 and ‖x‖²=1.

cases.query: The coefficient dot product equals the inner product for an arbitrary basis
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ take basis vector b₀=2 and x=y=1. The proposed coefficient dot product is 4 but the inner product is 1.

cases.query: For an arbitrary basis, the coordinate of x is ⟨bᵢ,x⟩
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ take b₀=2 and x=1. Its basis coordinate is 1/2, whereas ⟨2,1⟩=2.

cases.query: Every orthonormal coordinate change has determinant +1
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℝ the bases b₀=1 and c₀=-1 are orthonormal; the transition determinant is -1.

cases.query: Every real finite-dimensional endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Rotation by 90 degrees on ℝ² has no nonzero real eigenvector. Symmetry is essential; zero vectors do not qualify as eigenvectors.
